newsitem.title: USA: NZ National's role placates international markets.
newsitem.headline: NZ National's role placates international markets.

text.p: Widespread anxiety in the international business community over Winston Peters' rapid rise to prominence in New Zealand has eased with the maintenance of a Jim Bolger-led government, U.S. analysts said.
Most agreed that NZ First's decision to align with National rather than the Labour Party has helped temper international reaction to Peters' rise to Treasurer and Deputy Prime Minister.

Business leaders and the markets have also generally welcomed the easing in the New Zealand dollar, back from highs which gave it a short lived reputation on Wall Street as the new Swiss franc until most simply started calling it overvalued.
While the changes mapped out by the new economic regime have met a surprisingly neutral response, a number of economists warned Peters and the new coalition were still "on probation".

"We pretty well knew what was coming. It's one thing to spell it out, now we'll have to see how it is enacted," said Zurich Kemper Investments Inc. global analyst David Hale, a stern critic of Peters.
Economists in New York speculated what sort of reaction a NZ First-Labour alliance might have provoked.

"In the long run I'm sure it wouldn't have made much difference, but Bolger-(Bill) Birch and (Don) Brash had built good reputations here and it would have been a bit of a plunge into the unknown," said a New York-based New Zealand investment adviser who asked not to be named. "The house would probably be still shaking."

Richard Koss from investment firm Maria Fiorini Ramirez and Co. was surprised when Peters announced his decision. "It's interesting National are still there - that will keep things steady when there could have been (a reaction)," he said.

John Simpson from Goldman Sachs, a longtime admirer of the New Zealand Reserve Bank system, was pleased the hierarchy in the financial community remained relatively intact although he agreed the Kiwi dollar's strength would swiftly diminish.
"We've been bearish on the Kiwi for six months now," he said. "I think we've seen the peak and won't see it for some time again. Clearly they don't want the exchange rate to appreciate."

Merrill Lynch's Michael Rosenburg said the now vulnerable New Zealand dollar would find some support from the continued outflow of Japanese capital to the dollar bloc. "I'm sure Australia and New Zealand will get their share," he said.
Business leaders here were generally cautious and slightly sceptical, privately questioning how Peters would develop his role as Treasurer.

"Why they need a Treasurer, I've got no idea. He obviously wants to do something to make his mark on the economy. It makes me nervous," said one U.S.-based New Zealand businessman who asked not to be named.

Fletcher Challenge's North American representative Geoff Whitcher was upbeat, particularly about the easing of the dollar. "I think there comes a time when the high dollar reaches that stage where it hurts and we had definitely reached that," he said. Whitcher also pointed out that in "world terms" the changes in the New Zealand framework were relatively minor.
"People generally in the financial world here they are very sophisticated, they are dealing daily with changes in places like Russia and in Asia," he said.
"What is happening in New Zealand is small by comparison and probably somewhere in the centre.

"When you're in that hothouse atmosphere; stuck in the political centre of it all in Wellington, I think you tend to sort of lose that (global) perspective. Not too many judgments have been made. People are getting used to it."
Moody's Vice President senior analyst Yves Lamay re- iterated there was no threat to New Zealand's sovereign rating.
He said the ratings agency viewed the policy changes as "fine-tuning". -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 473-4746
